transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I suppose what finally brought me in is... I feel like the part of me that used to reach for people and actually take pleasure in things has just gone very quiet. I used to love my work, and I'd do yoga, go to art galleries, even journaling. Actually, speaking of journaling, I bought this absolutely gorgeous leather-bound notebook a few months ago from this little paper shop downtown. It's right next to that bakery that sells those incredible almond croissants. Have you ever been there? The baker is from Lyon, I think, or maybe it was Marseille, and he imports his butter directly from France. You can really taste the difference in the pastry layers, they just flake right off. I used to go there every Sunday morning before walking over to the modern art museum... but anyway, I haven't even opened the notebook. I don't go to the bakery anymore either. I’m mostly just... moving through my obligations now. Just waking up and doing what I have to do for my clients, and that's it.
Have you lost interest in activities that you used to enjoy, like your work, yoga, or visiting art galleries?

Yes, exactly. Like I was just saying, that whole part of me has just... gone quiet. I don't get any joy out of those things anymore. Take my yoga classes, for instance. I used to go to this beautiful little studio on 4th street. The instructor, Maya, she had this incredibly soothing voice, almost like a late-night jazz radio host, you know? And she would always play this Tibetan singing bowl at the end of the session. It resonated right in your chest. 

I actually looked into buying one of those bowls for my own office to use with my clients—they’re made of a special metal alloy, seven different metals, I think, supposed to represent the different planets or something. I spent a whole weekend just researching the acoustics of how they're hammered by hand in Nepal. 

But... well, anyway, I never bought it, and I haven't been back to Maya's class in months. It's just like I mentioned, the pleasure is gone. I'm just moving through my obligations now. I wake up, I handle my case files, and that's really it.
Do you feel down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

I wouldn't say I feel depressed, exactly. It's more of a... a flatness, I guess? Like the volume has been turned down on everything. But not really sad. Just... empty. Speaking of empty, I was actually looking at my calendar the other day, trying to figure out when I last had a full week of appointments. I use this physical planner, a really nice Moleskine one. Have you seen the ones with the weekly layout on the left and the ruled page on the right? They're brilliant for keeping track of client notes and court dates. I used to color-code everything with these fine-liner pens. I had a whole system—blue for family sessions, green for individual, red for anything court-mandated. I spent a fortune on those pens at this little art supply store that used to be over on Elm Street before it closed down. They had the best selection of imported stationery. But, um... what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I don't think I feel depressed most of the day. Just... flat.
Have you noticed a change in your energy levels or do you feel more fatigued than usual, even after resting?

Fatigued? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't feel physically tired, like I need to sleep more. My energy is fine, it's just... I don't know, unmotivated energy? Like a car idling. Actually, speaking of cars, my mechanic was telling me the other day about how idling too long can ruin your spark plugs. I take my sedan to this guy Tony over on 8th Avenue. He's fantastic, totally honest, which is so rare. He has this massive vintage Coca-Cola sign in his garage, the kind they used to paint directly on brick walls back in the fifties. I always wonder how he got it down and moved it there. The red paint is barely chipping. I've always loved that aesthetic, you know, the mid-century Americana. It makes you think of diners and jukeboxes. But anyway, no, I'm not unusually tired or fatigued. Just... idling, I suppose.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly than usual, or have others commented that you seem slowed down or, alternatively, that you're more restless or fidgety than before?

Moving slowly? No, I don't think so. I mean, I haven't noticed anything like that, and none of my colleagues have mentioned it either. I still walk at my normal pace. I actually used to walk to the family courthouse all the time for my custody hearings. It’s about a mile from my office, right past that new municipal building they just finished downtown. Have you seen the architecture on that place? They used this incredible pale limestone—imported from Indiana, I think. It’s supposed to weather really beautifully over time, kind of like those old European cathedrals that just look better the older they get. 

My grandfather was actually a stonemason back in the day, and he used to tell me all about how different rocks absorb water and change color. He had these huge, rough hands from working outside his whole life, and he could just look at a massive piece of granite and tell you exactly how it would split if you struck it with a chisel. We used to spend summers at his house up north, and he had this old wooden rowboat we'd take out on the lake right around sunset... 

But, um... sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, being fidgety or slowed down. No, no, I haven't noticed any changes like that. Just my normal pace.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite or weight recently?

Appetite? No, not really. I'm eating about the same as I always do. I usually just pack a lunch for the office, you know, a sandwich or a salad. Though I did recently find this incredible little bakery over on 4th Street that makes real, proper sourdough. Have you been there? They use a starter that the owner says is over fifty years old. It gives the bread this amazing, sharp flavor. I was talking to the baker—he’s this guy who used to work in corporate finance before he just dropped everything to bake bread—and he was telling me all about the fermentation process. It’s actually fascinating how the local humidity completely changes the way the yeast behaves. 

It made me think about when I tried baking my own bread back in grad school to manage my stress. I had this tiny, terrible oven in my apartment that would either underbake the center or scorch the bottom, no in-between. It was this old building with those gorgeous cast-iron radiators that just hissed and clanked all winter long. I used to put my boots on them to dry out after walking to my evening classes through the snow... 

Wait, sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my weight. No, no weight changes. My clothes all fit exactly the same.
